summary: Specifies an RTP payload format for 3GPP timed text, a time-lined, decorated text format stored in 3GP files. It can be synchronized with audio and video for uses such as captioning, titling, and multimedia presentations. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: Captions and titles for a video need to show up at the right moment. This explains how to send them over the internet in step with the picture.

questions: rtp payload format for 3gpp timed text
how to stream timed text over rtp
what are the rtp timed text unit types
subtitle: How to stream 3GPP timed text, such as captions and karaoke lyrics, in RTP packets alongside audio and video.

tldr.problem: 3GPP timed text (decorated, time-lined text such as captions) could be downloaded in 3GP files but had no RTP payload format, so it could not be streamed.
tldr.mechanism: Text samples, fragments and sample descriptions are wrapped in small 'units' with a 3-byte common header and one of five type-specific headers, and several units can be aggregated into one RTP packet.
tldr.outcome: Timed text can be streamed live or from a 3GP file in step with audio and video. The format is a Proposed Standard with no replacement listed.

today: RFC 4396 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2006, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Timed Text Payload Format
sections.content:
3GPP timed text is a media format for time-lined, decorated text, specified in 3GPP TS 26.245. Besides plain text it supports karaoke, scrolling text for newscasts and hyperlinked text, and it may or may not be synchronized with audio or video. The 3GPP packet-switched streaming service (PSS) allowed downloading timed text from 3GP files, but without an RTP payload format it could not be streamed.

RFC 4396 fills that gap. It covers streaming timed text read from a 3GP file and timed text generated in real time (live streaming).
sections.plainLanguage: You could already download subtitles with a video file, but you could not send them live. This RFC adds the missing way to send them while the video plays.

sections.title: Requirements and Limits
sections.content:
A 3GPP timed text file has four parts: layout information (kept in the Track Header Box), default formatting (the sample descriptions), the text strings in UTF-8 or UTF-16, and optional decoration called modifiers (highlight, blinking, karaoke, hyperlink, delay, style, text box position, wrap).

The payload format must support live streaming and streaming from a 3GP file, let a receiver rebuild a 3GP file, and allow sample descriptions to be sent out-of-band or in-band. It must also allow fragmenting a sample across packets, aggregating units into one packet and using resilience mechanisms such as repetition, retransmission or FEC.

To keep headers small, some maximums are lower than in 3GP files:

  • Text samples are limited to a 16-bit size, about 64 Kbytes, with no extension mechanism.
  • The sample description index is 8 bits; an extension mechanism exists.
  • Sample duration is 24 bits, about 4.6 hours at 1000 Hz; an extension mechanism exists.
  • Sample descriptions that do not fit a 16-bit size are not conveyed.
  • Only big endian UTF-16 is supported.
sections.plainLanguage: To keep the parcels small, the RFC sets size limits, like saying a postcard can only hold so many words. Those limits are big enough for captions.

sections.title: Units and Their Headers
sections.content:
Everything carried is a unit: a 3-byte common header followed by a type-specific header and then the sample contents. The common header has a U bit (0 for UTF-8, 1 for UTF-16, big endian), 4 reserved bits that must be zero, a 3-bit TYPE, and a 16-bit LEN counting every byte after the first one.

  • TYPE 1: one whole text sample. Fields: SIDX (sample description index), SDUR (24-bit duration in RTP timestamp units) and TLEN (length of the text string, so the receiver knows where modifiers start). LEN is at least 8, and an empty sample has LEN 8.
  • TYPE 2: a whole text string or a fragment of one, without modifiers. It adds TOTAL, THIS and SLEN (size of the whole original sample). LEN must be greater than 9.
  • TYPE 3: the whole modifiers or the first fragment of them. LEN must be greater than 6.
  • TYPE 4: a modifier fragment other than the first. LEN must be greater than 6.
  • TYPE 5: one sample description sent in-band. LEN must be greater than 3.

TYPE values 0, 6 and 7 are reserved. Receivers must discard units whose LEN breaks these rules, and must ignore units of an unrecognized type while still using the rest of the packet. A SDUR of zero means the duration is unknown, and the text is shown until the next sample becomes active.
sections.plainLanguage: Each piece of caption goes into a small envelope with a label saying what is inside: a whole caption, a piece of text, a piece of decoration, or the style rules. The label also says how long the envelope's contents are.

sections.title: Sample Descriptions and SIDX Values
sections.content:
Sample descriptions hold default formatting shared by many text samples. They can travel out-of-band (in SDP, reliably, once at setup) or in-band (in TYPE 5 units). The SIDX number links a sample to its description.

  • Static SIDX values, in the closed interval 129 to 254, name descriptions sent out-of-band that stay active for the whole session.
  • Dynamic SIDX values, in 0 to 127, name descriptions sent in-band. At most 64 can be active at once.
  • Values 128 and 255 are reserved.

When a session needs more than 64 dynamic descriptions, a wraparound mechanism keeps a sliding window of 64 active values and a guard interval of 64 inactive ones, so a reordered packet carrying a new description is not mistaken for an old one. Receivers must not overwrite an active description with a redundant copy. Sample descriptions are never fragmented.
sections.plainLanguage: The style rules are like a menu of numbered outfits. Captions just say which numbered outfit to wear, so the outfit itself only has to be sent once.

sections.title: Fragmentation, Reassembly and Aggregation
sections.content:
Timed text runs at low bitrates and samples are typically one or two hundred bytes, so fragmentation should be rare. If a sample can be sized to avoid it, that is preferred. When fragmentation is needed, text strings MUST be split at character boundaries so each piece can still be displayed, and the start of the modifiers MUST be marked with a TYPE 3 unit. Sample descriptions must not be fragmented.

Receivers group units by identical RTP timestamp and use TOTAL and THIS to order fragments and spot gaps; repeated units are used only once. A fragment is discarded if THIS is greater than TOTAL or TOTAL is zero. If text fragments are lost but modifiers arrived, the text can still be shown as plain text. The receiver also prepends the UTF-16 byte order mark 0xFEFF, which is never carried in RTP.

Units SHOULD be aggregated to save overhead, but only in three allowed orderings:

  • Zero or more TYPE 5 units, then zero or more TYPE 1 units.
  • Zero or more TYPE 5 units, then at most one TYPE 3 or TYPE 4 unit.
  • Zero or more TYPE 5 units, then at most one TYPE 2 unit, then at most one TYPE 3 unit from the same sample.

In an aggregate of TYPE 1 units, each later unit's timestamp is the previous unit's timestamp plus its duration. Empty samples can bridge gaps between non-consecutive samples. The marker bit is set to 1 when the packet has whole samples or the last fragment of a sample.

The default timestamp clock rate is 1000 Hz (RECOMMENDED), or the rate of an associated audio or video stream. The rate must be signaled out-of-band.
sections.plainLanguage: If a caption is too long for one envelope, it is cut between letters, never in the middle of one, and numbered like page 2 of 3. Short captions can share an envelope to save stamps.

sections.title: Resilience and Congestion Control
sections.content:
The simplest protection against packet loss is repetition. A server MAY resend the same payloads or some of their units, but a repeated unit MUST exactly match the original, with the same fragment boundaries and headers, and fragmentation is done once per sample. In a fully repeated packet only the RTP sequence number changes. Forward error correction and retransmission are mentioned as other options.

Congestion control follows RTP and its profile. The RFC notes that aggregation lowers overhead, while resilience schemes, repetition especially, raise the bitrate and must be counted.

The RFC works one newscast example in which a sample of about 8 seconds of text gives a 528-byte packet against a 576-byte MTU, and a redundant scheme sends 244-byte packets twice per second.
sections.plainLanguage: To make sure a caption arrives, you can send the same envelope more than once. That uses more mail capacity, so you must not overdo it.

sections.title: Media Type and SDP Usage
sections.content:
The payload is registered as media type video with subtype 3gpp-tt. Required parameters are rate and sver (supported versions of TS 26.245, default 60, meaning Release 6). Optional parameters include tx and ty (pixel offsets of the text track), layer (proximity to the viewer), width, height, max-w, max-h and tx3g, which carries base64-encoded static sample descriptions and MUST be used for sending them out-of-band.

In SDP, the media line uses m=video and the encoding line looks like a=rtpmap:<payload type> 3gpp-tt/1000. Parameters go in a=fmtp. Layout information MUST be conveyed reliably before the session starts, for example in an SDP offer/answer exchange. Unknown parameters are ignored. The RFC also gives how-to rules for unicast and multicast offer/answer use.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the show starts, both sides swap a short note saying where the captions go on screen and which outfit rules to use. This note is written in a standard form everyone understands.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The usual RTP security considerations apply. Two attacks are called out. A replay of an old packet carrying a sample description can invalidate the current set of active descriptions and corrupt the text display. Redundant fragments whose boundaries (LEN) or sample lengths (SLEN) differ from the originals might cause a decoder to crash.

Source authentication and integrity protection avoid both. The payload format itself provides no confidentiality, integrity or authentication, which must come from an outside mechanism such as SRTP.
sections.plainLanguage: A trickster could resend an old style note or send mismatched pieces to confuse the receiver. Locking the mail with an outside security system stops this.

fields.name: R
fields.desc: Reserved; must be zero and ignored by receivers.

fields.name: LEN
fields.desc: Bytes in the LEN field and everything after it in the unit.

items.label: TYPE 2
items.desc: A whole text string or a fragment, no modifiers.

items.label: TYPE 3
items.desc: Whole modifiers or the first modifier fragment.

items.label: TYPE 4
items.desc: A modifier fragment other than the first.
